items.text: Autistic burnout isn't laziness. It isn't a treatment-resistant depressive episode. It's what happens when accumulated load outpaces nervous-system capacity. That distinction changes everything about recovery.
items.rationale: Angle 1: names the two specific misreads clinicians and late-diagnosed adults most often encounter, then replaces them with precise language. Quotable and shame-dissolving without making any diagnostic claim.

items.text: You rested. You slept. You cancelled things. Still depleted. Rest doesn't resolve autistic burnout — reducing the load does. You can't recover while the weight stays the same.
items.rationale: Angle 2: the staccato opening mirrors the reader's own frustrated inner monologue before delivering the mechanism. Short rhythm, plain language, ends with a concrete implication not a platitude.

items.text: When you've masked for decades, what's left when you stop? That's not a rhetorical question. New peer-reviewed research calls it the unlearning–relearning journey — and it takes a while.
items.rationale: Angle 3: grounds a deeply personal experience in the 2026 Frontiers in Psychiatry paper without overselling its claims. Invites genuine replies rather than just resonance likes.

items.text: Discovering you don't know who you actually are — after decades of performing who others needed you to be — isn't a sign something went wrong. It's the beginning of finding out.
items.rationale: Angle 3 as pure validation rather than research hook. Evergreen and self-contained. The reframe in the final clause earns the post rather than just collecting recognition.

items.text: Fine at the party. Wrecked on Tuesday. That's the autistic social hangover — the delayed cost of masking, sensory load, and real-time social decoding. The gap between the event and the crash is part of the pattern.
items.rationale: Angle 4: the specific day-gap detail is the recognition hook that separates this from generic introvert-tiredness content. Naming three distinct cost sources ends the 'why am I like this' spiral.

items.text: The autistic social hangover arrives 1–3 days after the event, not during it. If midweek keeps collapsing on you after a good weekend, you're not falling apart. You're paying a bill that came late.
items.rationale: Angle 4 with a different frame — the delayed-billing metaphor makes the timing feel logical rather than mysterious, which is more emotionally useful than sympathy alone.

items.text: PDA demand avoidance isn't defiance. The nervous system reads an ordinary request as a threat and responds — automatically, not strategically. You can't reason someone out of a threat response.
items.rationale: Angle 5: 'automatically, not strategically' is the precise distinction that dissolves the power-play narrative and opens the door to compassion-first approaches without excusing specific behaviours.

items.text: Every 'please put your shoes on' escalating into a crisis isn't about the shoes. For a PDAer, the request itself registers as threat. It helps — a lot — to know the difference.
items.rationale: Angle 5 from the carer or co-parent perspective. Concrete household scene makes the abstract mechanism immediately recognisable. Non-clinical, opens empathy without prescribing a response.

items.text: Low-demand parenting for PDA gets called permissive all the time. What people miss: it demands more of the parent, not less — more regulation, more intentionality about what's truly essential.
items.rationale: Angle 6: directly corrects the most common misread without dismissing concerns. Highlighting the parental cost validates AuDHD parents dealing with their own nervous-system load simultaneously.
items.sensitivity_flag: Sits in a live debate — a counter-article ('Why Low-Demand Approaches Fail') is actively circulating. Post doesn't claim universal effectiveness, which keeps it defensible, but expect contention in replies.

items.text: You don't have to name a diagnosis to ask for a workplace adjustment. In many jurisdictions, describing the functional need is enough. 'I focus better with written instructions' is a complete request.
items.rationale: Angle 7: reframes disclosure as a spectrum rather than a binary all-or-nothing revelation, and hands readers a usable script they can act on this week. Changed 'most' to 'many' to avoid overstating legal universality.
items.sensitivity_flag: Legal protections vary significantly by jurisdiction and employer size. 'Many jurisdictions' hedges appropriately, but readers in precarious employment or outside well-legislated contexts should verify locally.

items.text: Body doubling works not because someone's watching. Shared presence lowers the nervous-system activation cost of starting a task. That's why the café, the silent co-worker, and the background TV all count.
items.rationale: Angle 8: the mechanism is the insight. Most people already do this instinctively without understanding why — naming it unlocks intentional, creative use and validates something they may have felt slightly embarrassed about.
items.sensitivity_flag: The co-regulation framing is community-supported and consistent with sourced material, but the precise neurological pathway is an active research area, not settled science. 'Lowers the activation cost' is behavioural language rather than a mechanistic claim, which keeps it defensible.

items.text: Working better with someone nearby — even silently — isn't dependency. That's co-regulation. And it's replicable: virtual sessions, background audio, a phone call that stays on. Build the scaffold you actually need.
items.rationale: Angle 8 as actionable follow-through: validates the instinct, names it accurately, then expands the toolkit beyond in-person presence. Ends with permission rather than instruction, which fits the voice.
